item.title: Team presentation ahead of 2027 Grand Départ will be a paid, ticketed event
item.description: The ASO announced on Monday that tickets will soon go on sale for the opening ceremony of the 2027 Tour de France, which will include the team presentation as well as entertainment from the organization that produces the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo. The festivities will take place at Edinburgh Castle
item.dc:creator: Dane Cash
item.content:encoded:
The ASO announced on Monday that tickets will soon go on sale for the opening ceremony of the 2027 Tour de France, which will include the team presentation as well as entertainment from the organization that produces the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo. The festivities will take place at Edinburgh Castle on Wednesday, June 30, ahead of the opening stage of the race on Friday, July 2.

General sale of tickets for the event, which start at £27, will open on October 30, although various pre-sale windows will open in advance of that date, including one for subscribers to the Grand Départ newsletter. According to Cycling Weekly, some 9,000 tickets are expected to be put on sale.

item.title: You should bring your bike
item.description: Any trip can be a bike trip if you're willing to put the work in. A veteran business traveler shares how to fit in a ride no matter where you are or why you're there.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Gordon
item.content:encoded:
Jon began racing in the early 1990s and stopped racing shortly thereafter. After hanging up the bike for a year, he got back in the saddle for the love of riding and ended up taking part in events like RAAM. He’s now looking forward to achieving fewer and fewer PRs on Strava as he gets older.

In February 2023, I was packing for a family trip to Montego Bay, Jamaica. I turned to my wife and said “so … mind if I bring my bike?” By that point, she was used to me making this ask, and the idiosyncrasies and occasional indignities of traveling with someone who will find any excuse to ride somewhere new. Fortunately, my wife is incredibly patient and understanding, and she knew about my cycling problem when she married me.

Two days later, breakfast buffet settling in my stomach, I rolled up to the guard at the front gate of the resort. After a brief back-and-forth with the guard – guests at Jamaican resorts are famously encouraged to remain on-premesis, for safety – I was allowed to pass with an “uh … be careful.”

And I was off. The coastal highway was right outside the gate, but despite its wide shoulder, the constant mid-day truck traffic made it unpleasant. Fortunately, Jamaica is a mountainous island, with plenty of steep, narrow roads with beautiful Caribbean views that wind around hills, farms, villages, and the occasional timeshare complex. Most of the roads had little or no traffic, and the only time I had to brake was for the goats and chickens that would wander across my path. Every time I passed someone – sitting on their porch, working in their garden – they would smile and wave.

I felt incredibly welcome, which is good, because I ended up on a more intense ride than I expected. Flower Hill climbed 1,100 feet in less than two miles (330 m in 3.2 km – roughly 10% average gradient), and the beautifully paved descent on the back side abruptly turned into a jeep track. And yet it was everything I sought in a vacation ride: I had the opportunity to see a part of a beautiful country that most visitors never get to experience.

Two days later, I found myself in an industrial parking lot at 5:30am as the local group ride assembled. I’d found it listed on the local club page on Strava. We rolled out, and Fowlie, Junior, Spider Man and I pacelined down the coastal highway, past sleepy beaches and fish shacks as the sun rose. We chatted, each of us sharing a bit about our lives and our years of cycling. I was even invited to ride in the local club race that weekend, and while I begged off due to the fact that I had not raced since 1998, I did get to watch the race when it passed our hotel.

Scratching the itch

I love riding my bike, I love to travel, and I particularly love riding my bike in new places. Over the years, I’ve tried all sorts of approaches to traveling with a bike, mostly to avoid airline bike fees: a bike with S&S couplers (TSA always messed up my careful packing when they inspected the bike), renting (worked pretty well until Rapha closed their clubhouses), and the Orucase Ninja (I just didn’t love removing my fork to pack my bike). But when United eliminated bike fees in 2021, the question around trip planning changed from “can I bring a bike?” to “is there any reason not to bring a bike?”

item.title: Soudal-Quick Step and Specialized part ways
item.description:
One of the longer-running team/equipment partnerships in the WorldTour is coming to an end as Soudal-Quick Step announced today that it's changing bike suppliers from Specialized to Merida.

The news is part of a broad equipment partner overhaul at the Belgian team that also includes
item.dc:creator: Joe Lindsey
item.content:encoded:
One of the longer-running team/equipment partnerships in the WorldTour is coming to an end as Soudal-Quick Step announced today that it's changing bike suppliers from Specialized to Merida.

The news is part of a broad equipment partner overhaul at the Belgian team that also includes switches to Continental tires, Prologo saddles, Sidi shoes and Lazer helmets. It's probably easier to list the partners who are continuing: Shimano and Castelli, notably. The switch brings to a close a relationship that dates back 14 seasons and coincided with some of the team's and bike brand's biggest successes, with wins in numerous Monuments, World Championships and Remco Evenepoel's double Olympic titles in 2024 and his 2022 Vuelta a España victory.

Evenepoel's own departure to Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe last offseason was likely a significant precipitating event for the bike brand swap. Evenepoel has a lifetime contract with Specialized, signed earlier this year, and that relationship is also reportedly part of the reason the 2023 merger attempt with Jumbo-Visma did not come to pass. Without Evenepoel's presence, Specialized has less reason to stay at a team whose marquee riders are largely sprinters. For Merida, however, it represents a path back to the WorldTour after sitting out a year after Bianchi took its place with Bahrain Victorious.

item.title: Decathlon adds climbing firepower with O'Connor, Sivakov, and De Plus
item.description: Decathlon-CMA CGM announced three big signings on Tuesday, headlined by the return of Ben O'Connor. The 30-year-old Australian, who raced with the team from 2021 to 2024 before a two-year stint with Jayco-AlUla, is heading back to Decathlon on a two-year deal.
item.dc:creator: Dane Cash
item.content:encoded:
Decathlon-CMA CGM announced three big signings on Tuesday, headlined by the return of Ben O'Connor. The 30-year-old Australian, who raced with the team from 2021 to 2024 before a two-year stint with Jayco-AlUla, is heading back to Decathlon on a two-year deal.

He will be joined in his new digs by Laurens De Plus, who is coming over from Netcompany-Ineos on a two-year contract, and Pavel Sivakov, who is making the move from UAE Team Emirates-XRG on a three-year a deal. All told, the acquisitions mark a substantial boost for Decathlon's GC ambitions. O'Connor in particular has finished second overall at the Vuelta a España, and all three riders give the team more firepower as Decathlon looks to build around rising star Paul Seixas.

item.title: Garmin's latest releases include a new flagship 1060 computer
item.description:
Garmin has expanded its cycling range with three new products, including a flagship 1060 computer, a Tacx Nēra indoor smart trainer and new Edge Explore 3 head units.

The headline launch is the Edge 1060, Garmin’s latest premium cycling computer. It adds a built-in microphone
item.dc:creator: Alex Hunt
item.content:encoded:
Garmin has expanded its cycling range with three new products, including a flagship 1060 computer, a Tacx Nēra indoor smart trainer and new Edge Explore 3 head units.

The headline launch is the Edge 1060, Garmin’s latest premium cycling computer. It adds a built-in microphone and speaker, allowing riders to use voice commands to report hazards, select routes and request ride data. Navigation has also been updated with route previews and alerts for road closures and hazards. Its US$800 / £700 / €800 retail price is US$100 / £100 / €100 more than the 1050 it replaces, while battery life remains at a claimed 20 hours with no solar option joining the range.

Alongside the 1060, Garmin has released a new indoor trainer, the Tacx Nēra. It features multidirectional movement and claimed power and cadence accuracy within one per cent, and is available with a standard freehub or Zwift Cog and Click. Both versions cost US$1,000 / £860 / €1,000.

The final products are the Edge Explore 3 and Edge Explore 3 Plus, offering navigation, ride data and e-bike compatibility via a touchscreen display. The Explore 3 costs US$400 / £350 / €400, while the Plus, which adds voice-command functionality, costs US$500 / £430 / €500.

item.title: Burgaudeau to Burgos Burpellet BH
item.description:
TotalEnergies has not had an encouraging year, with many speculating that this would be the French team's last season, despite team boss Jean-René Bernaudeau's recent claim that the team "will be at the next Tour de France".

Another canary in the coal
item.dc:creator: Iain Treloar
item.content:encoded:
TotalEnergies has not had an encouraging year, with many speculating that this would be the French team's last season, despite team boss Jean-René Bernaudeau's recent claim that the team "will be at the next Tour de France".

Another canary in the coal mine: one of its most loyal and loved riders, Mathieu Burgaudeau, has signed a contract with the Spanish ProTeam Burgos Burpellet BH, joining former TotalEnergies teammates Thomas Bonnet and Mattéo Vercher on the purple-clad team. Other big names from TotalEnergies have moved elsewhere: Anthony Turgis to XDS-Astana and Jordan Jegat to Lidl-Trek.

Burgaudeau has been a popular animator of breakaways over the years, and has a versatile, punchy style that is reminiscent of the likes of Julian Alaphilippe – right down to the two looking quite similar. Burgaudeau's career includes a stage win at Paris-Nice, second at the Tour de Doubs, as well as stage wins and the general classification at the Tour of Istanbul. He is also one of our personal favourites at Escape Collective Towers.

Burgaudeau was a surprise omission from TotalEnergies at the Tour this year, and in the announcement of the move said “I’d like to thank the Burgos Burpellet BH team for giving me the chance to get back on track next year. I’m really looking forward to winning races and finishing among the leaders in those events that suit my riding style. The team will give me the opportunity to show what I’m capable of on different terrains and to take part in a great racing programme.”

Notably, Burgos Burpellet BH appears on the UCI's recently-published list of teams that have applied for a ProTeam license in 2028; TotalEnergies does not, setting the French team up for a race to secure sponsors and UCI ratification before time runs out in mid-December.

item.title: 'We needed to make some hard decisions': Why EF let Richard Carapaz go
item.description: Team boss Jonathan Vaughters tells Escape that higher costs and budget cutbacks ultimately led to the decision to part ways with Richard Carapaz.
item.dc:creator: Dane Cash
item.content:encoded:
Gruber Images, Cor Vos

Big names change teams every transfer season, but it's not every day that a squad lets its best rider out of an already existing contract to head elsewhere. Even if mid-contract transfers are becomingly increasingly common in pro cycling, they remain the exception to the rule, especially for riders who are thriving – which is why the news that Richard Carapaz is leaving EF Education-EasyPost for NSN raised eyebrows last week.

The 33-year-old Ecuadorian, a former winner of the Giro d'Italia and the Olympic road race, was easily his team's top-ranked rider in 2026, a season that saw him claim his second career king of the mountains title at the Tour de France along with two stage wins there and a top-five overall at the Vuelta a España. He was also reportedly under contract for two more seasons. Talents like that don't grow on trees, so what could have led to his split with EF?

item.title: Picnic-PostNL and Jayco-AlUla miss 2027 registration deadline
item.description: The UCI released the list of first- and second-division teams that met the deadline for submitting registration paperwork for the 2027 season on Monday with Picnic-PostNL and Jayco-AlUla absent from the list of on-time WorldTour applicants on both the men's and women's
item.dc:creator: Dane Cash
item.content:encoded:
The UCI released the list of first- and second-division teams that met the deadline for submitting registration paperwork for the 2027 season on Monday with Picnic-PostNL and Jayco-AlUla absent from the list of on-time WorldTour applicants on both the men's and women's sides.

For Jayco, this marks the second straight year the organization has been late to file its paperwork, while Picnic is coming to the end of its unusual one-year WorldTour license period after the UCI did not grant its squads licenses for the standard three-year term at the start of the current promotion/relegation cycle.

In a statement, the UCI said that teams missing the registration deadline, "still have the possibility to rectify their situation before the end of the registration process, which would enable them to be registered for the 2027 season. In accordance with the UCI Regulations and subject to other applicable provisions, riders from these teams may terminate their contracts early, but this right will lapse if their team is subsequently registered.

"The final list of teams registered for the 2027 season will be published by the UCI on 8 December 2026, at the end of the registration procedure."

item.title: Takeaways as Swenson and Gomez Villafañe take fourth Life Time Grand Prix titles
item.description: Two familiar champions, but very different seasons: Swenson scraped back the men's title while Gomez Villafañe once again proved almost impossible to beat.
item.dc:creator: Alex Hunt
item.content:encoded:
Josh Weinberg, Velocio

Big Sugar took place this past weekend in Bentonville, Arkansas, bringing the 2026 Life Time Grand Prix series to a close and drawing a line under its fifth season as the premier independent (of the UCI) off-road race series.

At the top of the 25-rider men's and women's overall standings were two familiar faces, with Keegan Swenson and Sofia Gomez Villafañe both taking their fourth Grand Prix overall titles, racing for Specialized Off-Road Racing.

Gomez Villafañe ended her season with a second place behind Stella Hobbs, finishing 1:43 down on the 33-year-old American. Swenson, meanwhile, finished 13th, 3:40 behind Martins Blums.

While Gomez Villafañe remains as hard to beat as ever, capable of winning across a range of race situations and terrains, Swenson's latest title was anything but straightforward. Just one point separated him from Brendan Johnston in the final standings – raising the question of whether, five years into the Life Time GP, the landscape is shifting.

A single point

Keegan Swenson may have only failed to finish on the top step of the podium at the Life Time Grand Prix once – last year, when Cam Jones went from wild-card entry to Unbound winner and ultimately season champion. However, while he might be back on the top step, Swenson's dominance wasn't quite so convincing in 2026.

That may have been partly down to the injuries he sustained early in the season after being doored on a training ride in Girona, Spain. Swenson had been due to race the Cape Epic shortly afterwards, but withdrew from that event after being diagnosed with a fractured pelvis and other related complications. It was around six weeks before he was given the all-clear to return to training, leaving him with little time to prepare for the opening round at the Sea Otter Classic around a month later.

Swenson came out swinging at Sea Otter, though, suggesting the crash hadn't hampered his form as much as many expected. He finished second, only being pipped to the line by Bradyn Lange.
